text: According to the book, what precise property distinguishes a continuous temporal order (modeled on the real numbers) from a merely dense one (modeled on the rational numbers)?
choices: Continuity requires that time have adjacent moments, whereas a dense order never does
Continuity requires a smallest temporal unit, whereas a dense order is infinitely divisible
Continuity adds completeness — every bounded Cauchy sequence converges to a limit within the ordering — filling the gaps a dense order might leave
Continuity makes time only partially ordered, whereas a dense order is totally ordered
explanation: Both dense and continuous orders are infinitely divisible, with no adjacent moments and no smallest unit; the difference is completeness — continuous time (the reals) fills every gap so that all bounded Cauchy sequences converge within it, whereas a dense-but-incomplete order (the rationals) can leave 'holes.' Options 0 and 1 wrongly import discreteness features, and option 3 confuses this with the total-versus-partial-order distinction.
